name: Raspberry
lede: Raspberry is the red of the berry, a vivid purplish red, and one that naturalists were matching to fruit long before it was an everyday color name.

sections.title: A fruit's name
sections.body:
*Raspberry* is the berry's name used for its color. Paterson's dictionary defines the French *framboise* as the red of the raspberry [1]. In English, Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates the color name to 1892, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it as block 256, a vivid purplish red [6]. St Clair's glossary calls it a rich pinky red, the color of the berry [5].

Not every raspberry is the same one. The swatch here is #B00149, while Wikipedia's raspberry is a brighter, pinker #E30B5D [6]. Its nearest named neighbors are [[amaranth-purple]] (duller), [[cranberry]] (darker), [[rose-red]], [[rouge]] and the redder [[raspberry-red]], all within about 5 units [6].

sections.title: The berry as a yardstick
sections.body: Naturalists used the berry as a reference long before the dictionaries did. In Syme's 1821 edition of Werner's color nomenclature, carmine red, number 91, is illustrated among plants by [[flower:raspberry|raspberry]], cockscomb and carnation pink, and among minerals by the Oriental [[gem:ruby|ruby]] [2]. The next red, lake red, is shown by the red tulip, the rose and [[gem:spinel|spinel]] [2]. A fruit and a stone stood side by side as the same red.

sections.title: Berries, stones and dyes
sections.body:
Jewelers borrowed the berry as well. Finlay lists rhodolite, a pinkish [[gem:garnet|garnet]], among the stones sometimes called raspberry garnets [3].

St Clair mentions amaranth, an azo dye first made in the 1880s and described as raspberry-hued [5]. By her account it still colors maraschino cherries in Europe as E123, and it has been banned in America over cancer concerns [5]. As a color word, she adds, amaranth has lost any consensus, and may now mean cherry, grape or plum [5]. The nearest of our colors, [[amaranth-purple]], is exactly this kind of drifted name.

Pastoureau, explaining why green stands for youth, points to ripening: berries and cherries pass from green to red, and plums and blackberries go on to blue or black [4]. Raspberries are among the fruits he names at the red stage.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, one work has a color within six units of this swatch over at least five per cent of the canvas: Kirchner's [[painting:nga-76206|Two Girls under an Umbrella]] (1910), where it covers 13 per cent [7]. That makes it rarer than 86 per cent of the named colors we track [7].

The word has a long, uneven history in print: used as an adjective in Google Books, it peaks in the 2010s [8]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [7].

origin.first_recorded: Maerz and Paul 1930 date the color name to 1892 (per the library notes); ISCC-NBS 1955
origin.source: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour; library notes

disambiguation.gloss: a redder, more orange raspberry from another list

questions.q: In Syme's 1821 edition of Werner, which plants illustrate carmine red?
True or false: every raspberry swatch in our sources is the same color.
Which garnet is sometimes called the raspberry garnet?

openers: Before dictionaries listed raspberry as a color, Werner's red chart used the berry to show carmine.
Raspberry garnets exist: rhodolite is a pinkish garnet sometimes sold under that name.
Only one painting in our archive of 23,781 has a big patch of this exact raspberry, as photographed.

issues: Fixed Pastoureau 'middle stage' inference: he lists raspberries at the red stage
